mandrasuchus:study:1.title: New alligatorid, Mandrasuchus milleri , from the Early Paleocene (Danian) of the Denver Basin supports earliest Paleocene North American alligatorid radiation (Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, 2026)

facts.statement: The holotype of Mandrasuchus is specimen DMNH EPV.48541, which includes a skull, tail, osteoderms, and limb fossils.
facts.quote: specimen DMNH EPV.48541, consisting of a skull, tail, osteoderms, and a number of limb fossils, serving as the holotype in the 2026 description by Lessner and colleagues.

facts.statement: The species name milleri honors Ian Miller, who discovered many specimens at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science.
facts.quote: The species name "milleri" comes from Ian Miller, who was responsible for the discovery of many specimens while working at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science.

facts.statement: Mandrasuchus lived during the Danian stage of the Paleocene.
The type locality of Mandrasuchus is the Denver Formation.
Fossils of Mandrasuchus have been found in the United States.
Fossils of Mandrasuchus have been found in Colorado.
The fossil range of Mandrasuchus is the Early Paleocene (Danian).
Mandrasuchus is the oldest confirmed alligatorine, appearing within the first million years after the K-Pg event.
facts.quote: It represents the oldest confirmed alligatorine, appearing in the fossil record within the first million years following the K-Pg event.

facts.statement: Mandrasuchus was likely a macro-generalist predator capable of eating large prey and crushing the shells of molluscs, crustaceans, and turtles.
facts.quote: It seems to have reached a length of up to 2 m and may have been a macro-generalist predator, capable of both feeding on relatively large prey while also using its more globular posterior teeth to crush the shells of molluscs, crustaceans and perhaps turtles.

facts.statement: Mandrasuchus is an extinct genus of alligatorine.
facts.quote: Mandrasuchus is an extinct genus of alligatorine from the earliest Paleocene Corral Bluffs (Denver Formation) fossil site Colorado, USA.

facts.statement: Mandrasuchus was recovered as a member of the subfamily Alligatorinae.
facts.quote: Mandrasuchus was recovered as a member of the subfamily Alligatorinae, possibly a close relative of Allognathosuchus mooki and Wannaganosuchus.

facts.statement: Lessner and colleagues favor a phylogenetic topology that treats Navajosuchus specimens as separate and unconstrained.
facts.quote: Ultimately, Lessner and colleagues favor the topology recovered by treating the three specimens that traditionally make up Navajosuchus as separate and without constraints.

facts.statement: It is debated whether teeth and osteoderms found near the K-Pg boundary in Weld County belong to Mandrasuchus, as similar dentition exists in Late Cretaceous crocodilians.
facts.quote: However, a number of other crocodilians with similar dentition are known from the Late Cretaceous northern hemisphere, making the assignment of the aforementioned teeth to Mandrasuchus less than certain.

facts.statement: Mandrasuchus reached about 2 meters, which is slightly smaller than the 2.3-meter Borealosuchus specimens found at Corral Bluffs.
facts.quote: Among these, Mandrasuchus is slightly smaller than Borealosuchus, reaching only 2 m compared to the 2.3 m achieved by Corral Bluffs Borealosuchus specimens (although members of the species are known to reach 3 m in other parts of North America).

facts.statement: The heterodont dentition of Mandrasuchus suggests a macro-generalist diet similar to modern alligators, allowing it to eat various prey and crush shells.
facts.quote: The teeth of animals like Madrasuchus could also indicate a macro-generalist diet similar to that seen in modern alligators, with the heterodont dentition both allowing the animal to go after the same prey as other generalists while also giving it the ability to crunch through the shells of molluscs, crustaceans and turtles.

facts.statement: There is some evidence suggesting Mandrasuchus exhibited burrowing behavior.
facts.quote: In at least one case, there seems to be some evidence for burrowing behavior in Mandrasuchus.
